title: Why God made man needy
source_text: Ἑξῆς τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος, θέλων μὴ μᾶλλον ἡμῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν πεποιηκέναι τὰ φυόμενα ἐπὶ γῆς ἢ τοῖς τῶν ζῴων ἀγριωτάτοις, φησίν· ἡμεῖς μέν γε κάμνοντες καὶ προσταλαιπωροῦντες μόλις καὶ ἐπιπόνως τρεφόμεθα· τοῖς δ᾿ „ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα πάντα φύονται,“ οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι πανταχοῦ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην σύνεσιν γυμνάζεσθαι βουλόμενος ὁ θεὸς, ἵνα μὴ μένῃ ἀργὴ καὶ ἀνεπινόητος τῶν τεχνῶν, πεποίηκε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπιδεῆ· ἵνα δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐπιδεὲς αὐτοῦ ἀναγκασθῇ εὑρεῖν τέχνας, τινὰς μὲν διὰ τὴν τροφὴν ἄλλας δὲ διὰ τὴν σκέπην. καὶ γὰρ κρεῖττον ἦν τοῖς μὴ μέλλουσι τὰ θεῖα ζητεῖν καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν τὸ ἀπορεῖν ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῇ συνέσει χρήσασθαι πρὸς εὕρεσιν τεχνῶν. ἤπερ ἐκ τοῦ εὐπορεῖν πάντῃ τῆς συνέσεως ἀμελεῖν. ἡ τῶν κατὰ τὸν βίον γοῦν χρειῶν ἀπορία συνέστησε τοῦτο μὲν γεωργικὴν τοῦτο δὲ ἀμπελουργικὴν τοῦτο δὲ τὰς περὶ τοὺς κήπους τέχνας τοῦτο δὲ τεκτονικὴν καὶ χαλκευτικὴν, ποιητικὰς ἐργαλείων ταῖς ὑπηρετουμέναις τέχναις τὰ πρὸς τροφήν· ἡ δὲ τῆς σκέπης ἀπορία τοῦτο μὲν ὑφαντικὴν τὴν μετὰ τὴν ξαντικὴν καὶ τὴν νηστικὴν εἰσήγαγε τοῦτο δὲ οἰκοδομικὴν. καὶ οὕτως ἀναβέβηκεν ἡ σύνεσις καὶ ἐπὶ ἀρχιτεκτονικήν. ἡ δὲ τῶν χρειῶν ἔνδεια πεποίηκε καὶ τὰ ἐν ἑτέροις τόποις γεννώμενα φέρεσθαι διὰ ναυτικῆς καὶ κυβερνητικῆς πρὸς τοὺς μὴ ἔχοντας ἐκεῖνα· ὥστε καὶ τούτων ἕνεκεν θαυμάσαι τις ἂν τὴν πρόνοιαν, συμφερόντως παρὰ τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐνδεὲς ποιήσασαν τὸ λογικόν. τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλογα ἑτοίμην ἔχει τὴν τροφὴν. ἅτε οὐδ᾿ ἀφορμὴν πρὸς τέχνας ἔχοντα· καὶ φυσικὴν δ᾿ ἔχει τὴν σκέπην. τετρίχωται γὰρ ἢ ἐπτέρωται ἢ πεφολίδωται ἢ ὠστράκωται. καὶ ταῦτα δὲ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν ἡμῖν λελέχθω τῆς φασκούσης λέξεως παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ· ἡμεῖς μὲν κάμνοντες καὶ προσταλαιπωροῦντες μόλις τρεφόμεθα· τοῖς δ᾿ „ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα πάντα φύονται.“
pass_a_gloss: Next to these Celsus, wishing that providence has not more for us made the things growing on earth than for the most savage of animals, says: We indeed, toiling (κάμνω) and laboring hard (προσταλαιπωρέω), with difficulty (μόλις) and laboriously (ἐπιπόνως) are fed (τρέφομαι); but for them unsown (ἄσπαρτα) and unploughed (ἀνήροτα) all things grow; not seeing that God, wishing everywhere to exercise (γυμνάζω) human understanding (σύνεσις), so that it might not remain idle (ἀργή) and uninventive (ἀνεπινόητος) of the arts (τέχναι), has made man needy (ἐπιδεής); so that through his very neediness he might be compelled (ἀναγκάζω) to find (εὑρίσκω) arts, some for food, others for shelter (σκέπη). For it was better for those not about to seek the divine things (τὰ θεῖα) and to philosophize (φιλοσοφέω) to be at a loss (ἀπορέω) in order to use understanding for discovery (εὕρεσις) of arts, than from having plenty (εὐπορέω) in every way to neglect (ἀμελέω) understanding. — The want (ἀπορία) of the needs (χρεῖαι) of life at any rate (γοῦν) established (συνίστημι) now agriculture (γεωργική), now vine-culture (ἀμπελουργική), now the arts about gardens (κῆποι), now carpentry (τεκτονική) and smithing (χαλκευτική), makers of tools (ἐργαλεῖα) for the arts that serve (ὑπηρετέω) things for food; and the want of shelter introduced (εἰσάγω) now weaving (ὑφαντική), the one after carding (ξαντική) and spinning (νηστική), now house-building (οἰκοδομική); and thus understanding has climbed up (ἀναβαίνω) even to architecture (ἀρχιτεκτονική). And the deficiency (ἔνδεια) of needs has made also the things produced in other places to be carried through seafaring (ναυτική) and piloting (κυβερνητική) to those not having them; so that also for these one might admire (θαυμάζω) providence, which advantageously (συμφερόντως) made the rational (τὸ λογικόν) needy compared to (παρά) the irrational animals. For the irrational have food ready (ἑτοίμη), since they have no starting-point (ἀφορμή) toward arts; and they have natural (φυσική) shelter; for they are haired (τριχόω) or feathered (πτερόω) or scaled (φολιδόω) or shelled (ὀστρακόω). — And let these things be said by us for defense (ἀπολογία) against the saying (λέξις) in Celsus: We toil and labor hard and barely are fed; but for them unsown and unploughed all things grow.
pass_b_english: Next, Celsus, wishing to maintain that providence made what grows on the earth no more for us than for the most savage of the animals, says: “We, for our part, toiling and labouring hard, feed ourselves barely and with great effort, while for them ‘all things grow unsown and untilled’ (Homer, Odyssey 9.109).” He does not see that God, wishing to exercise human understanding on every side, so that it might not stay idle and never devise the arts, made man needy, so that by his very neediness he might be compelled to find out arts, some for food and others for shelter. For it was better for those who were not going to seek things divine and to pursue philosophy to be in want, so that they would use their understanding to find out arts, than to have plenty of everything and neglect their understanding.

At any rate, the lack of what life needs brought into being farming, vine-dressing and the arts of gardening, and also carpentry and smithing, which make tools for the arts that serve the getting of food. The lack of shelter brought in weaving, which comes after carding and spinning, and also building; and so understanding rose even to architecture. And want of necessities has caused the things produced in other places to be carried, by seafaring and the pilot’s art, to those who do not have them. So for these reasons too one might admire providence, which, for our good, made the rational being needier than the irrational animals. For the irrational animals have their food ready to hand, since they have not even a starting point for the arts; and they have a natural covering, for they are clad with hair or feathers or scales or shells.

Let this, then, be said by us in defence against the passage in Celsus that says: “We, for our part, toiling and labouring hard, barely feed ourselves, while for them ‘all things grow unsown and untilled.’”

repeated Celsus quotation aligned with first rendering

Celsus’s words: “We, for our part … unsown and untilled.” (repeated at the end, with μόλις but without καὶ ἐπιπόνως). Within them he quotes Homer, Odyssey 9.109 (of the land of the Cyclopes), set off in single quotation marks. ἅτε οὐδ᾿ ἀφορμὴν πρὸς τέχνας ἔχοντα: ἀφορμή taken as ‘means, starting-point’; rendered ‘since they have not even a starting point for the arts’. The τοῦτο μὲν … τοῦτο δὲ list markers are rendered as a plain list. The repeated quotation at the end mirrors the first rendering, minus καὶ ἐπιπόνως. ὑφαντικὴν τὴν μετὰ τὴν ξαντικὴν καὶ τὴν νηστικὴν: weaving that follows carding and spinning. No Scripture quoted.
